title: Tenant fairness routing lattice and multi-region control plane notes
content:
Summary:

This is a working note that pulls together a compact policy model for tenant- and org-aware routing that meets multi-region SLAs while giving predictable cost/latency tradeoffs and operational controls for noisy neighbors. The aim is a small set of control plane primitives that are expressive enough to capture reserved vs best-effort capacity, hierarchical quotas, and graceful preemption/eviction across regions.

Motivation and goals:
- Avoid noisy neighbor outages: ensure a single large customer or runaway workload cannot cause disproportionate tail latency for others.
- Respect contractual commitments: reserved capacity and SLA tiers must get guaranteed access (to a defined extent) even under contention.
- Predictable degradation model: when capacity is tight we prefer graceful, observable degradation (throttles, quality preserving fallbacks) over opaque failures.
- Multi-region affinity: prefer local region capacity but allow overflow to other regions per policy (cost/latency aware).
- Operational simplicity: runtime policy surface should be small, debuggable, and supported by tracing/metrics.

Key constraints we must handle:
- Heterogeneous resource types: some tenants use embeddings-heavy workloads, others generation; packing constraints differ.
- Per-tenant state explosion: we cannot maintain heavy state per tenant in hot path; must rely on hierarchical rules + sampled telemetry.
- Legal/geography: certain tenants cannot egress certain regions.
- Burstiness: tenants can have short bursts that should be absorbed without breaking long-term fairness.

High-level model (priority lattice):
- Each tenant has a tuple of attributes: {org_tier, reserved_tokens, burst_allowance, regions_allowed, eviction_priority}.
- org_tier: enum {enterprise, business, standard, free} influences baseline priority and routing choices.
- reserved_tokens: long-running commitment (monthly/annual) expressed as reserved RPS or tokens/sec per model class.
- burst_allowance: short-term token budget to allow spiky traffic (leaky bucket semantics).
- eviction_priority: numeric hint used when preemption is needed (lower number -> evict first).
- Policies compose with overrides: org-level > project-level > route-level. The lattice orders requests by (is_reserved ? reserved_priority : baseline_priority) then by org_tier then by arrival_time/age for fairness within equivalence classes.

Control plane primitives to implement:
1) Reservation leases: long-lived allocations recorded in control plane: capacity slice per region and model class. Leases expire if not renewed and can be transferred.
2) Soft-quotas (token buckets): per-tenant, per-model-class token buckets enforced at edge routers with burst allowance metrics exposed.
3) Best-effort pool: capacity not reserved becomes best-effort and scheduled using fair-share within eligibility.
4) Preemption rules: when reserved demand exceeds reserved supply, preemption is limited to eligible best-effort workloads; reserved tenants should not be preempted except in extreme emergency with manual/auto escalation.
5) Cross-region overflow: policy flag per-tenant allowing overflow to other regions with cost_multiplier and max_latency_budget; control plane routing will prefer same-region but can divert when local p95 exceeds threshold.
6) Circuit-breakers & backpressure signals: runtime emits per-node overload signals that immediately throttle best-effort and signal to control plane for heavier action.

Quota model details:
- Two-layer quotas: guaranteed (reservation) and elastic (shared). Guaranteed is door-keyed to contracts. Elastic is shared and subject to fair-share.
- Implementation approach: store reservations in the control plane DB (compact rows: tenant, model_class, region, guaranteed_tokens, burst_cap). At edge we cache leases with TTL and a version hash for fast checks.
- Enforcement: a lightweight local token check on request arrival. On token exhaust: if request is tagged reserved, place in short enqueue (prefetch) for small wait; if best-effort, either reject or route to lower-cost variant.

Noisy neighbor detection and automated mitigation:
- Detection signals: sustained increase in preemption events, sharp p99 delta vs baseline, token bucket saturation > X% for Y minutes, long KV-cache thrashing counts.
- Mitigation actions (escalating):
  1) soft-throttle best-effort routes (reduce burst_allowance)
  2) spill to cheaper/quantized model variant (if enabled)
  3) auto-scale dedicated pool if tenant is configured for burst billing
  4) degrade sampling rate / reduce logging for noisy tenant (cheap but visible)
  5) in-flight eviction (preemption) of low-priority best-effort requests
  6) notify on-call + customer-success (human-in-loop for enterprise)
- Metrics we need: per-tenant p50/p95/p99 latency, token consumption rate, cache hit rate, queued requests length, preemption_count, cross-region-redirects.

Multi-region routing and data locality:
- Region affinity is the default. Policy fields: preferred_regions (ordered), allowed_regions (set), deny_regions (set), cross_region_cost_multiplier.
- Decision flow on request: 1) if preferred region has available reserved tokens -> route local; 2) if local reserved exhausted but allowed_regions have reserved -> route to least-cost allowed region within latency budget; 3) otherwise use best-effort pool (local preferred) and apply fair-share; 4) if no capacity and tenant allows overflow -> attempt cross-region with reduced quality or quantized model.
- Geo-legal constraints: control plane must expand policy record with required data residency tags and edge routers must consult these tags before any cross-region routing.

Operational playbook (outline):
- Normal: monitor reserved/best-effort utilization; ensure reserved pools are under 80% to absorb bursts; set auto-scale triggers for dedicated pools.
- Burst detected: soft-throttle best-effort, notify owning SRE/eng, open incident if p99 > SLA and reserved tenants impacted.
- Noisy neighbor: if mitigation steps fail, temporarily reduce burst_allowance and enable preemption; follow-up with customer-success and solutions engineering to tune reservation or billing.
- Contention across regions: use fallback policy to route user-facing traffic to next-best region if latency cost within per-tenant max_latency_budget; use background replication for stateful workloads if supported.

Example scenarios (short):
1) Enterprise tenant with reservation in us-west hits sustained +30% traffic: control plane honors reservation, auto-scale dedicated pool if configured for burst, otherwise overflow to us-east if allowed; notify account team.
2) Startup tenant with no reservation floods CPU with heavy long-context generations: edge sees token saturation, best-effort throttles back, runtime replaces model with 8-bit quantized variant for best-effort requests, and preempts low-priority jobs.
3) Mixed embeddings & generation tenant: route embeddings to CPU-optimized regional fleet with reservation and generation to GPU pool; if embedding pool saturated, spill embeddings to shared CPU pool with possible higher latency.

APIs and data model notes (control plane surface):
- /leases (GET/POST/PUT): manage reservations.
- /quota-check (fast edge RPC): returns {allowed:true|false, reason, new_tokens, version_hash}. Keep response small and cachable.
- /overflow-policy (GET): per-tenant overflow settings.
- /telemetry (streaming): per-tenant aggregated consumption and alarms.
- DB row shape (compact): tenant_id | model_class | region | guaranteed_tokens | burst_cap | allowed_regions | eviction_priority | last_renewed (but keep as flat fields in DB; no complex nested docs).

Rollout and migration plan (practical):
- Phase 0: implement token-bucket enforcement at edge for a small pilot of 10 tenants (mix of tiers) using a feature flag.
- Phase 1: add reservation leases and control plane UI for ops to see usage vs reservation. Integrate with billing data.
- Phase 2: enable cross-region overflow for tenants who opt-in; add cost-multiplier accounting.
- Phase 3: automated noisy-neighbor mitigation rules + SLO-linked alerts and remediation runbooks.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- How aggressively do we preempt reserved tenants in extreme situations? Do we build escalation windows and billing-based preemption?
- Edge state vs central lookups: how long can we safely cache lease state before staleness causes oversubscription?
- Cost visibility: should cross-region overflow automatically bill to tenant at a premium, or route to account and let CS negotiate?
- Model-aware packing: can we cheaply approximate packing constraints across heterogeneous model families to improve multi-tenant packing without heavy scheduling?

Next steps / action items:
- Aisha: prototype token-bucket enforcement in edge router (PR linked).
- Diego: sketch DB migration plan for reservation rows and TTL-based cache.
- Ben: add telemetry dashboard (per-tenant token burn + p99 delta).
- Rita: coordinate with CS to define allowable cross-region defaults for enterprise customers.

Notes to self / loose thoughts:
- Want to keep runtime fast-path as a simple allow/deny + small enqueue; heavy decisions (preemption, lease rebalancing) should be async in control plane.
- Consider a predictive component later: detect upcoming bursts from traffic patterns and pre-warm other regions.
- Work with finance to wire signal for auto-billing on cross-region overflow to simplify ops.
- Keep an escape hatch: global conservative circuit-breaker that makes the system fail-safe to critical enterprise traffic.

References and bookmarks:
- Confluence: Tenant Capacity Model (linked above)
- Slack: #platform-routing (thread: noisy-neighbor-jan-2026)
- GitHub: prototype edge quotas PR (linked above)
- Jira: JIRA-PLT-812 (follow-up: reservation DB schema)

End of note.
